Jane admitted that the engagement surprised her a little. But she said less about her surprise than about her sincere wish for their happiness, and Elizabeth could not persuade her that they were unlikely to be happy. Kitty and Lydia felt no envy of Miss Lucas, since Mr. Collins was only a clergyman. The matter meant nothing to them beyond being news they could spread in Meryton.

Lady Lucas could hardly help feeling triumphant now that she could remind Mrs. Bennet, in her turn, of the comfort of having a daughter marry well. She visited Longbourn rather more often than usual to say how happy she was, although Mrs. Bennet’s sour expressions and unkind remarks might have been enough to drive happiness away.

An awkwardness between Elizabeth and Charlotte kept both of them silent on the subject. Elizabeth felt certain they could never truly confide in each other again. Her disappointment in Charlotte made her turn with greater affection to her sister. She was sure nothing could ever shake her faith in Jane’s goodness and sensitivity. She also grew more anxious each day about her sister’s happiness: Bingley had now been away a week, with no news of his return.

Jane had answered Caroline’s letter promptly and was counting the days until she could reasonably expect another. Mr. Collins’s promised letter of thanks arrived on Tuesday, addressed to their father. His gratitude was expressed with all the solemn ceremony that a year’s stay with the family might have deserved. Having satisfied his conscience on that point, he went on, in many delighted phrases, to announce his happiness at winning the affection of their charming neighbour, Miss Lucas. He then explained that he had accepted their kind invitation to visit Longbourn again so readily only because it would allow him to enjoy her company. He hoped to return two weeks from Monday. Lady Catherine, he added, approved of his marriage so warmly that she wanted it to take place as soon as possible. He trusted that his dear Charlotte would find this an impossible argument to resist when asked to choose an early date for making him the happiest of men.

Mrs. Bennet no longer took any pleasure in the prospect of Mr. Collins returning to Hertfordshire. Instead, she was as ready as her husband to complain about it. It was very strange that he should stay at Longbourn instead of Lucas Lodge; it was also very inconvenient and a great deal of trouble. She hated having guests in the house when her health was so poor, and people in love were the most disagreeable visitors of all.

We spent several sorrowful hours waiting for eleven o’clock, when the trial was to begin. My father and the other members of the family were required to appear as witnesses, and I went with them to the court. Throughout that miserable travesty of justice I endured a living torment. The question to be settled was whether my curiosity and unlawful contrivances would bring about the deaths of two fellow creatures: the one a smiling infant, all innocence and happiness; the other murdered in a manner far more dreadful, burdened with every circumstance of disgrace that could stamp the murder with unforgettable horror. Justine, too, was a worthy girl, endowed with qualities that promised her a happy life; now everything was to vanish into a shameful grave, and through my doing! A thousand times would I sooner have declared myself guilty of the crime laid to Justine’s charge; but I had been away when it occurred. Such a confession would have been taken for a madman’s ravings and would not have cleared the girl who suffered on my account.

Justine’s bearing was composed. She wore mourning, and the solemnity of her emotions lent her face, always pleasing, an exquisite beauty. She seemed nevertheless assured of her innocence and did not shake, though thousands stared at her and cursed her. Whatever kindness her beauty might otherwise have awakened had been erased from the spectators’ minds by their conception of the monstrous deed she was believed to have done. She remained calm, but the effort behind her calmness was plain; since her earlier bewilderment had been cited as evidence of guilt, she compelled herself to present an air of courage. On coming into court she glanced about and soon found the place where we sat. At the sight of us a tear appeared to cloud her eye; she mastered herself at once, however, and her expression of mournful tenderness seemed to bear witness to her complete innocence.

The proceedings opened, and when the advocate prosecuting her had set out the accusation, several witnesses were summoned. A number of curious circumstances joined against her, sufficient to unsettle anyone who lacked the proof of her innocence that I possessed. She had stayed out all night when the murder was committed. Near morning a market-woman had seen her close to the place where the murdered child’s body was subsequently discovered. Asked by the woman what she was doing there, she had looked exceedingly strange and given only a bewildered, incomprehensible reply. She reached the house at about eight o’clock; when someone asked where she had spent the night, she answered that she had been searching for the child and anxiously demanded whether there was any news of him.

“Come on, Tom,” I said, “you could at least tell a person. What’s a bar sinister?”

“Oh, I don’t know. But he has to have one. All the nobility do.”

That was just like him. If he didn’t feel like explaining something, he wouldn’t. You could keep asking for a week and it wouldn’t change a thing.

He’d settled all that business about the coat of arms, so he went on to finish the rest of that part of the job: working out a sorrowful inscription. He said Jim needed one, like they all did. He invented a whole lot, wrote them down on a sheet of paper, and read them out like this:

“Here a captive heart burst.”

“Here a poor prisoner, abandoned by the world and his friends, wasted away his sorrowful life.”

“Here a lonely heart broke, and a weary spirit found its rest, after thirty-seven years imprisoned alone.”

“Here, homeless and friendless, after thirty-seven years of bitter imprisonment, died a noble stranger, the illegitimate son of Louis XIV.”

Tom’s voice shook as he read, and he nearly broke down. When he finished, he couldn’t possibly decide which one Jim should scratch onto the wall; they were all so good. At last he decided he’d let him scratch them all. Jim said it would take a year to scratch all that stuff onto the logs with a nail, and besides, he didn’t know how to write letters. Tom said he’d draw the letters out for him, and then all Jim would have to do was follow the lines. A little later he said:

“Now I think of it, logs won’t work. Dungeons don’t have log walls. We have to carve the inscriptions into a rock. We’ll bring a rock.”

Jim said a rock was worse than the logs. He said carving them into a rock would take such an awful long time that he’d never get out. But Tom said he’d allow me to help him. Then he took a look at how Jim and I were getting on with the pens. It was terribly tedious, difficult work, and slow, and it gave the sores on my hands no chance to heal. We hardly seemed to be making any progress at all, so Tom said:

“I know how to sort this out. We need a rock for the coat of arms and the sorrowful inscriptions, and we can kill two birds with that same rock.
